STATE OF VERMONT 
PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION 
Case No. 23-0561-TF 
Petition of Vermont Gas Systems, Inc. for a 
change in rates and use of the System 
Expansion and Reliability Fund for an overall 
0.1% increase in rates effective April 1, 2023 
ORDER APPROVING RATE CHANGE AND  
USE OF REMAINING MONIES IN THE SYSTEM EXPANSION AND RELIABILITY FUND 
I.
INTRODUCTION
This case involves the Vermont Public Utility Commission’s (“Commission”) 
investigation into Vermont Gas Systems, Inc.’s (“Vermont Gas” or the “Company”) tariff filing 
requesting a 10.7% increase in non-gas rates (daily access and distribution charges) and the 
withdrawal of all remaining funds from the System Expansion and Reliability Fund (“SERF”) 
for an overall 0.1% increase in rates.1   
The Commission must determine the non-gas rate components of Vermont Gas’s cost of 
service, or the base rate, as well as the return on equity (“ROE”).  Based on our review of the 
evidentiary record developed in this case and the arguments presented by the parties, we 
determine that a 10.13% increase for non-gas costs should be approved effective for bills 
rendered on or after November 1, 2023, resulting in an overall firm rate decrease of 0.3%. 
II.
PROCEDURAL HISTORY
On February 15, 2023, Vermont Gas filed a petition requesting a 10.7% increase in non-
gas rates to be effective April 1, 2023.  Vermont Gas requested that the Commission suspend the 
effectiveness of the proposed tariffs pursuant to Section 226(a) with implementation occurring 
on November 1, 2023, after the conclusion of the Section 227(a) seven-month review period.  
Vermont Gas also requested use of the remaining $670,000 in the SERF to reduce the cost of 
service.  When combined with a forecasted 14.9% reduction in natural gas charges, the overall

effect on rates would be a 0.1% rate increase.  Consistent with the Company’s approved

III. 
LEGAL STANDARDS 
Traditional rate cases filed pursuant to 30 V.S.A. § 225 are subject to the “just and 
reasonable” standard.2  The Vermont Supreme Court explained the process for determining just 
and reasonable rates as follows: 
The [Commission] seeks to establish utility rates for the immediate future that will 
allow investors a reasonable return without overcharging the ratepayers.  As the first 
step in arriving at a fair rate of return, the [Commission] determines the operating 
expenses and the “rate base”—the utility’s net plant investment—for the “test 
year,” usually the most recent full calendar year . . . .  The [Commission] then 
adjusts the rate base by modifying the test year rate base to reflect “known and 
measurable” changes in plant investment.  These are changes that are measurable 
with a reasonable degree of accuracy and have a high probability of being in effect 
in the adjusted test year . . . .  Finally, the [Commission] calculates an appropriate 
return on the adjusted rate base and devises adjusted rates that will produce a fair 
rate of return on the company's property in the immediate future.3  
 
Adjustments for operating expenses and capital investments are generally subject to the “known 
and measurable” standard, which allows changes that are “measurable with a reasonable degree 
of accuracy and have a high probability of being in effect in the adjusted test year.”4  In 
traditional rate proceedings, it is the utility’s responsibility to satisfy this standard: “the burden of 
supporting [a] change in rates or rate structure [rests] squarely on the proponent utility.”5 
 
2 Petition of Village of Hardwick Elec. Dept., 143 Vt. 437 (1983) (“By statute, the  [Commission] is required to 
set rates that are just and reasonable.”). 
3 In re Green Mountain Power Co., 162 Vt. 378, 380–81 (1994). 
4 Central Vermont Public Service Co., Dockets 6946 & 6988, Order of 3/29/05 at 67. 
5 In re Consolidated Rate Appeals of Green Mountain Power Co., 142 Vt. 373, 381 (1983); see also In re Green 
Mountain Power Co., 162 Vt. at 386.

In Bluefield Waterworks v. Public Service Commission, the United States Supreme Court 
set certain constitutional limitations that guide Commission review of a traditional rate 
proceeding.6  Specifically, the Bluefield Court held: 
A public utility is entitled to such rates as will permit it to earn a return on the value 
of the property which it employs for the convenience of the public equal to that 
generally being made at the same time and in the same general part of the country 
on investments in other business undertakings which are attended by corresponding 
risks and uncertainties; but it has no constitutional right to profits such as are 
realized or anticipated in highly profitable enterprises or speculative ventures.  The 
return should be reasonably sufficient to assure confidence in the financial 
soundness of the utility and should be adequate, under efficient and economical 
management, to maintain and support its credit and enable it to raise the money 
necessary for the proper discharge of its public duties.7 
 
The Vermont Supreme Court, in interpreting Bluefield, opined that “[r]ates cannot be set 
so low as to be confiscatory for the utility nor so high as to be excessive for the consumer . . . . 
Between these extremes lies a ‘zone of reasonableness’ within which a regulatory commission is 
free to set rates without judicial intervention.”8  In previous decisions, we have recognized that 
“it is the ‘substance and effect’ of the [Commission’s] actions which must bear judicial scrutiny.  
The United States Supreme Court has taken the same view of utility regulation by establishing 
that it is the ‘end result’ which must meet the constitutional test.”9 
Under Bluefield, a utility does not hold a right of return, but is instead entitled to a “fair 
opportunity to earn a reasonable rate of return.”10  Moreover, longstanding Vermont law 
authorizes “the Commission to consider management efficiency and customer service in arriving 
at a determination of just and reasonable rates.”11  Thus, we follow the above legal standards set 
by the United States Supreme Court, the Vermont Supreme Court, and the Commission in 
deciding this case.

IV. 
FINDINGS 
1. This case addresses the non-gas rate components of Vermont Gas’s cost of service.  
These components are the daily access and distribution charges.  Collectively, these charges are 
considered base rates.  The natural gas charge component of Vermont Gas’s rates is modified on 
a quarterly basis pursuant to the purchase gas adjustment approved in Case No. 22-5085-PET as 
part of the Company’s Alternative Regulation Plan.  Matthew Mitchell, Vermont Gas 
(“Mitchell”) pf. at 5; Sean Foley, Department (“Foley”) pf. at 2. 
2. Vermont Gas’s Alternative Regulation Plan includes a rate-smoothing mechanism 
that will spread the impact of the non-gas rate change in this case over the three-year term of the 
Plan.  Mitchell pf. at 6. 
3. The test year is the 12-month period ending December 31, 2022, and the rate year is 
the 12-month period from October 1, 2023, through September 30, 2024.  Mitchell pf. at 6. 
4. The cost of service for the rate year is determined by evaluating the actual costs 
incurred by the Company during the test year and adjusting those costs based on expected 
changes in the rate year.  Mitchell pf. at 6. 
5. The cost of service consists of operating and non-operating costs.  Operating costs are 
the expenses that the Company incurs to operate its system for customers, such as transmission, 
distribution, and sales.  Non-operating costs are associated with Vermont Gas’s investments in 
its natural gas pipeline network and other capital investments that support the provision of 
service to customers.  Mitchell pf. at 6. 
6. Vermont Gas’s initial proposed revenue requirement for non-gas costs was 
$66,524,399, an increase of 10.7%.  Exh. VGS-MM-1. 
7. Vermont Gas proposes to use the rate-smoothing adjuster approved as part of its 
alternative regulation plan to reduce the overall change in non-gas costs from 10.7% to 
approximately 6.4%.  The portion of the rate change not recovered in FY2024 would be 
accounted for with a regulatory asset that would be amortized over the term of the three-year 
plan.  McNeil pf. at 5-6. 
8. Vermont Gas’s proposal reflects the withdrawal of the remaining $670,163 from the 
SERF.  Exh. VGS-MM-1.

9. Vermont Gas’s proposal also reflects inflationary pressures and other changes to non-
operating costs, such as taxes and interest rate increases.  Vermont Gas’s operating costs are 
about 7% higher than in the previous rate case, consistent with the 7% increase in the Consumer 
Price Index for all items in the Northeast in 2022 versus 2021.  McNeil pf. at 4. 
10. Transmission-related expenses in the Rate Year will not change from the Test Year.  
Although the work performed during the Rate Year will vary from the Test Year, the costs are 
expected to remain constant.  Mitchell pf. at 8-9. 
11. Distribution-related expenses in the Rate Year will decrease from the Test Year to 
account for non-labor-related expenses of approximately $173,000.  This decrease is driven by 
adjustments in two distribution-related areas and associated accounts: (1) Distribution Mains – 
Maintenance and (2) Other Equipment related expenses.  Mitchell pf. at 9. 
12. Vermont Gas’s computer expenses are proposed to increase by $279,300, mostly 
related to improving and modernizing information technology systems to gain efficiency and 
improve processes and to update infrastructure to harden against cybersecurity risks.  Mitchell 
pf. at 11. 
13. The termination of the SERF and inflationary cost increases together account for 
nearly 70% of the Company’s proposed rate change.  McNeil pf. at 4-5. 
14. The remaining changes are driven by non-operating costs, including depreciation 
expense, taxes, and the cost to finance rate base.  McNeil pf. at 5. 
15. Non-operating costs include categories such as depreciation, property taxes, and 
recovery of carrying costs.  The methodology for determining rate base in this cost of service is 
essentially unchanged from previous rate proceedings.  The cost-of-service rate base reflects the 
13-month average from September 2023 to September 2024.  The starting point for the rate base 
calculation is the per book account values as of December 31, 2022.  These values are then 
adjusted for changes from January 2023 to September 2024.  The total proposed rate base for the 
Rate Year is $272 million.  Mitchell pf. at 16. 
16. The ROE of 9.34% initially proposed by Vermont Gas is based on the indexing 
method used in previous cases, which is tied to fluctuations in the yield rate of 10-Year United 
States Treasury Notes.  The baseline is the ROE approved in Vermont Gas’s last rate case, which

was set based on the same methodology.  In that case, Case No. 22-0480-TF, the Commission 
approved an ROE of 8.92%.  This ROE change accounts for approximately 12% of the proposed 
increase in non-gas rates.  McNeil pf. at 5, 11; Mitchell pf. at 21. 
17. Vermont Gas’s proposed cost of- service reflects an overall weighted cost-of-capital 
of 7%, which is based on a 50% equity ratio and reflects Vermont Gas’s total outstanding long-
term and short-term debt obligations.  Mitchell pf. at 18. 
18. The Department engaged experts to review the Company’s proposed cost of service 
and ROE.  Foley pf. at 2. 
19. Based on that expert review, the Department recommends several adjustments to the 
cost of service that would result in a 9.91% increase to Vermont Gas’s non-gas rates.  Total 
required non-gas revenue would be $66,052,348.  Foley pf. sur. at 1; exh. PSD-SF-2. 
20. In adjustment PSD-3, the Department recommends removing $407,811 in 
unamortized debt expense from rate base, which would result in a cost-of-service reduction of 
$36,472.  Unamortized debt expenses are the administrative fees incurred by a utility to secure a 
loan.  Hunt pf. at 19. 
21. Debt expense reflects those costs that are necessary to obtain debt, such as the 
transactional costs associated with applying for and closing on debt issuances.  McNeil pf. reb. at 
21. 
22. The parties agree that debt expense is a necessary cost “incurred at the outset as part 
of the process of obtaining a loan,” and that “the amortization of the debt expense for the 
duration of the loan is appropriate.”  Hunt pf. at 18. 
23. At the time that Vermont Gas obtains a loan, these expenses are not included in the 
debt amount, nor are they included in Vermont Gas’s annual operating expenses.  Vermont Gas 
pays the debt expenses up front and then recovers that cost by amortizing the expenses over the 
life of the loan.  McNeil pf. reb. at 21. 
24. If the debt expense is removed from rate base as proposed by the Department, 
Vermont Gas would pay the debt expense up front and recover it from customers over time, but 
would not recover the time value of the debt expense.  McNeil pf. reb. at 21; tr. 8/24/23 at 21 
(McNeil).

25. In adjustment PSD-6, the Department recommends removing from rate base the 
“Pension, Net” regulatory asset and any related accumulated deferred income taxes (“ADIT”) 
and adjust the pension expense in Vermont Gas’s cost of service from ($165,000) to $0.  
Hoffman pf. sur. at 3, 13. 
26. The “Pension, Net” regulatory asset reflects pension contributions that Vermont Gas 
has made but not yet recovered from customers.  McNeil pf. reb. at 6.  
27. The “Pension, Net” regulatory asset consists of (1) Vermont Gas’s net pension 
obligation, which is the difference between the amount that Vermont Gas has recorded as 
pension expense and the amount of that recorded pension expense that Vermont Gas has actually 
contributed to the pension trust, net of (2) the SFAS158 measurement adjustment.  Hoffman pf. 
at 15. 
28. SFAS158 is a U.S. Generally Accepted Accounting Principle (“GAAP”) mandate that 
requires employers to annually remeasure the “funded status” of their pension plans and to 
reflect that funded status as an asset or liability on its balance sheet.  Hoffman pf. at 16. 
29. As part of a process to de-risk its pension plan, Vermont Gas has been working 
toward bringing its pension plan to a fully funded status.  One way in which Vermont Gas has 
worked on this goal is by making contributions to the pension fund in excess of normal pension 
expense—in excess of the amount collected in rates.  McNeil pf. reb. at 26. 
30. As part of its proposed cost of service, Vermont Gas included both additional pension 
income that results from excess pension contributions and the asset that reflects pension 
contributions not yet recovered from customers.  McNeil pf. reb. at 26-27. 
31. Vermont Gas did not provide any cost-benefit analysis to support its position that 
making excess contributions to its pension fund (i.e., payments in excess of what would 
otherwise be required under GAAP requirements) provides a benefit to VGS’s ratepayers.  
Hoffman pf. reb. 9-11. 
32. Vermont Gas adopted the Department’s proposal to adjust rate base downward by 
$177,783 ($245,947 offset by tax impact of $68,164) to account for an error in the Company’s 
initial calculation in the cost of service. McNeil pf. reb. at 4. 
33. The parties agree that a 9.24% ROE is appropriate.  Tr. 8/24/23 at 30 (McNeil).

34. After incorporating the agreed-upon ROE of 9.24% but without accepting the 
Department’s two proposed adjustments described above, Vermont Gas’s proposed non-gas 
revenue requirement would be $66,183,631, a 10.13% increase.  Exh. VGS-ALM-2; tr. 8/24/23 
at 30 (McNeil). 
V. 
DISCUSSION 
The parties agree on most elements of Vermont Gas’s cost of service, including the 
Company’s capital structure and a return on equity of 9.24%.  We approve those aspects of the 
cost of service upon which the parties have reached agreement. 
There remains disagreement regarding two adjustments supported by the Department.  
We discuss those adjustments, in turn, below.  We also briefly address a proposed condition 
regarding a future lead-lag study. 
Unamortized Debt Expense 
 
Vermont Gas has included $407,811 of unamortized debt expense in rate base, which 
increases its cost of service by $36,472.  The parties agree that debt expenses, which are incurred 
as part of the process of obtaining loans, are a necessary component of its investment in assets.  
Including unamortized debt expenses in rate base, Vermont Gas argues, accounts for the time-
value of Vermont Gas’s up-front payment of debt expenses.  Excluding those expenses, 
according to Vermont Gas, will result in an under-recovery.  Vermont Gas also argues that 
including unrecovered debt expenses in rate base follows the same methodology that has been 
approved by the Commission in past rate cases.   
 
The Department agrees that Vermont Gas is permitted to recover its debt expenses and 
that debt expenses are appropriately amortized over the life of the loan to which they relate, but 
does not agree that Vermont Gas should earn a return on the unamortized balance of debt 
expenses by including the amount in rate base.  The Department argues that debt costs are not an 
investment in operating assets but should instead be accounted for as part of the cost of debt, 
which is done in other regulatory jurisdictions, such as the Federal Energy Regulatory 
Commission (“FERC”).  The Department also notes that, although the Commission has approved

Case No. 23-0561-TF 
 
Page 10 
 
 
Vermont Gas’s inclusion of debt expenses in rate base in past cases, it has never directly 
addressed the issue. 
 
We agree that, to the extent that the Commission has approved the inclusion of debt 
expenses in rate base in the past, the issue was not identified by the parties or specifically 
addressed by the Commission. 
In raising the issue in this case, the Department cites to several FERC decisions for the 
principle that a utility “is entitled to a return of the refinancing costs, but not on the refinancing 
costs.”12  Based on our review of those decisions, the Department appears to be correct that 
FERC does not allow utilities to include unamortized debt expenses in rate base.   
Although FERC does not allow utilities to include debt costs in rate base, it does provide 
an alternate method for utilities to recover the time-value of their debt expenses.  FERC’s 
regulations require utilities to account for debt expenses in the debt-cost component of the cost 
of capital using the “yield to maturity” (“YTM”) method.13  FERC describes the YTM method as 
follows: 
[T]he yield to maturity is the interest rate that, when applied to the net proceeds, 
will provide payments equal to the present value of the interest payments on the 
bond plus the present value of the par value of the bond. . . .  The reason is that the 
YTM method provides for recovery of the par value of the bond, not just recovery 
of the net proceeds.  The difference between the two is equal to the issuance costs, 
and that amount is recovered under the YTM method.  The yield to maturity method 
thus provides the amounts necessary to pay off a current debt and the expenses in 
issuing the current debt.  Consequently, the YTM method provides for the full 
recovery of the cost of current long-term debt.14 
 
FERC further describes the YTM calculation that should be applied pursuant to its regulations:

¶61,040 at ¶ 584 (2013)). 
13 See Enbridge Pipelines (KPC), Order on Initial Decision, 100 FERC ¶61,260, 61,963 (“This is the method

it should be granted an exception.”) (the Enbridge order is included in the record as Exh. PSD-SDH-8). 
14 Id.  Although Vermont Gas argues that these cases apply to unique situations different from the debt expenses 
involved here (Vermont Gas Reply Brief at 3), Enbridge Pipelines addresses two separate situations—the first of 
which is the same as presented by Vermont Gas.  See id. at ¶61,963 (“There are two types of debt costs at issue here.  
The first is the cost of current long-term debt which includes the cost of the principal amount, and costs associated 
with current long-term debt such as issuance expenses, discounts, and premiums.  The second type is costs 
associated with debt that has been reacquired.”).

The Commission’s regulations state that the yield to maturity is based on the 
interest rate and the net proceeds of outstanding debt. . . .  Using the YTM method, 
the interest rate is the rate that, when applied to the net proceeds [e.g., the debt 
amount less expenses due to issuing that debt], will provide payments equal to the 
present value of the interest payments plus the present value of the par value of the 
debt.15 
 
In discovery, Vermont Gas asked the Department how it should treat unamortized debt 
expenses and received the following response:   
VGS would use the Net Proceeds approach to determine the cost of the debt rate 
for each long-term loan reported at Schedule 11, column (7).  To determine the cost 
rate, the numerator is determined by identifying the annual interest expenses, 
amortized debt expense, amortized discount or premium and amortized gain or loss 
on reacquired debt.  The denominator is determined by computing the long-term 
debt Gross Proceeds less unamortized debt expenses, discount, premium, or gain or 
loss on reacquired debt.16 
Neither Vermont Gas nor the Department proposed an adjustment to the cost of service 
based on changing the effective cost of debt as described in Enbridge Pipeline and the 
Department’s discovery response.  When questioned about Vermont Gas’s ability to recover the 
time-value component of its debt expenses at the evidentiary hearing, the Department’s witness 
pointed to other mechanisms in the ratemaking process such as construction work in progress 
(“CWIP”) or allowance for funds used during construction (“AFUDC”).  These mechanisms, the 
witness argued, allow a utility to recover its costs of financing during the construction period for 
an asset funded by debt.17  The Department has not recommended requiring Vermont Gas to 
recalculate its effective cost of debt using the YTM method, leaving only the requested exclusion 
of debt expenses from rate base. 
Without an alternative method of recovery, the exclusion of unamortized debt expenses 
from rate base will not allow Vermont Gas to recover the full value of its debt expenses at the 
time the expenses were incurred.  Without adjusting the effective cost of debt, Vermont Gas is 
left with an up-front present-value expense that would be amortized over the debt period and 
 
15 Id. 
16 Exh. VGS Cross-1. 
17 Tr. 8/24/23 at 47-49 (Hunt).

Page 12 
 
 
recovered from future, less valuable funds.18  While Vermont Gas would recover the dollar 
amounts of those debt expenses, it would lose the time value of the expenses because they would 
be repaid in future dollars. 
We disagree that AFUDC or CWIP alone provides a recovery of the time value of debt 
expenses, which is consistent with FERC allowing either AFUDC or CWIP for asset investments 
not yet in service and debt expenses through the YTM method.  By accounting for the cost of net 
invested capital and debt expenses, AFUDC or CWIP works in tandem with the YTM method to 
provide a complete return of utility investments and associated expenses. 
The parties have not identified a specific methodology for accounting for debt expenses 
that is required for Vermont utilities.  FERC’s YTM method is required by regulation.  The 
closest Commission precedent, however, approves a methodology similar to FERC’s YTM 
method: 
Another issue relating to the cost of the Company’s debt is the appropriate treatment 
of the amortization of debt discount and gain.  The Company deducts from its 
outstanding total debt an amount for unamortized debt expense which results in 
increasing the effective interest rate.  The Public takes the expense of a debt issue 
and accounts for it as an operating expense spread over the years the debt will be 
outstanding.  We agree with the method followed by the Company, which reflects 
in the rate the fact that most of the bond issues were sold at less than par value.19 
 
Although the details of the calculation are not described in the order, the approved 
method of using net debt proceeds to calculate a higher effective interest rate that accounts for 
debt expenses is similar to the YTM method followed by FERC and described by the 
Department in its discovery response.  The rejected proposal of amortizing debt issuance 
expenses as an operating cost is what will occur if we require Vermont Gas to exclude the 
unamortized debt expense balance from rate base.   
The record does not support a calculation under a YTM or other method such as what 
was approved in Docket 4230.  Although the Department recommended the YTM approach in 
 
18 See In re Vermont Yankee Nuclear Power Corp., Docket No. 6545, Order of 7/26/02 at 8 n.17 (“Money in the 
future isn’t worth as much as money right now, and to pretend it’s worth the same amount is to miss a big part of the 
analysis.”). 
19 Petition of Central Vermont Public Service Corporation, No. 4230, Order of 12/8/78 at 27 (cited by Vermont 
Gas in its initial brief).

discovery, neither Vermont Gas nor the Department recommended in evidence that the 
Commission adopt the YTM approach or submitted revised cost-of-service calculations.20  We 
are thus left to decide between the options presented by the parties. 
As an initial point, we note that the amount of the reduction and the effect on the rates 
under the Department’s recommended approach is small.  The parties agree that removing 
unamortized debt expenses from rate base at an ROE of 9.34% would reduce Vermont Gas’s 
proposed non-gas cost of service of $66,373,261 by $36,472, or approximately 0.06%.21  This 
reduction, however, would add up over the life of each debt instrument and result in a continuing 
under-recovery of debt expenses by Vermont Gas, which we prefer to avoid.  As a point of 
comparison, the reduction to the non-gas cost of service from Vermont Gas agreeing to the 
Department’s proposed ROE of 9.24% is 0.31%, or approximately $186,316 based on Vermont 
Gas’s current non-gas revenue.22 
Similarly, the impact of allowing Vermont Gas’s debt expenses to remain in rate base—
as has apparently occurred for years without objection—is also small.  Leaving debt expenses in 
rate base will slightly increase Vermont Gas’s non-gas cost of service, but so would the increase 
to the weighted cost of capital under the YTM method.  Vermont Gas’s recovery of its 
unamortized debt expenses will increase its non-gas cost of service whether accounted for 
through the YTM method or by including it in rate base. 
We conclude that allowing Vermont Gas to include its unamortized debt expenses in rate 
base provides a better accounting of debt-expense costs than would excluding them without any 
other adjustment.  While the 0.06% cost-of-service increase may not precisely match the increase 
that would occur if debt costs were recalculated using the YTM method, the increase is less than 
the decrease from the agreed-upon ROE reduction.  The resulting cost of service with

Pension, Net 
 
The Department challenges Vermont Gas’s proposal to collect from ratepayers excess 
contributions that Vermont Gas has made to its pension fund as part of a “de-risking” strategy to 
bring its pension plan to fully funded status. 
 
The Department recommends that Vermont Gas be required to “exclude the ‘Pension, 
Net’ regulatory asset (and any related ADIT) and adjust the pension expense it includes in the 
revenue requirement from $(165,000) to $0.”24  In support of this recommendation, the 
Department argues that Vermont Gas has not provided documentation or quantifiable 
calculations to demonstrate that Vermont Gas’s excess pension contributions will result in 
ratepayer benefits.  The Department also challenges Vermont Gas’s assertions regarding full 
funding and sale of its pension plan to a third party as speculative and not supported by detailed 
cost-benefit analyses.  The Department further argues that testimony and discovery responses 
provided by Vermont Gas in this case indicate that “[Vermont Gas] made an executive decision

discussed: 
The standard that [the Commission] has used to determine the prudence of utility 
decisions and actions is long-standing and clear.  Prudence is judged according to 
whether a utility’s actions were reasonable and prudent in light of circumstances at 
the time, based on what the utility knew or should have known.  A prudence 
determination is not based on hindsight or knowledge that was only available after 
the decision in question.  A prudence determination acknowledges the managerial 
rights of the utility, but cannot merely presume the reasonableness of management. 
Instead, the utility is held responsible for taking all reasonable steps to acquire 
relevant information and to respond appropriately.30 
With respect to the used-and-useful standard, we have made clear that “[a] long-standing 
principle of regulatory law has been that an investment must be used and useful for the provision 
of public service before the public should be asked to bear its cost.”31  Whereas the “known and 
measurable” standard assesses whether a utility’s proposed rate adjustment is “measurable with a 
reasonable degree of accuracy and [has] a high probability of being in effect in the adjusted test 
year,”32 the prudence and used-and-useful standards have been used to assess historically 
incurred costs.33 
 
Although we agree with Vermont Gas that the prudence and used-and-useful standards 
provide the appropriate framework for assessing this issue, we do not share Vermont Gas’s 
conclusion that the evidentiary record in this case is sufficient to make a conclusive 
determination under either standard with respect to the excess pension contributions.  As

Lead-Lag Study 
 
In its testimony, the Department recommended that Vermont Gas be required to conduct 
a new lead-lag study.  In support of this recommendation, the Department argued that Vermont 
Gas’s most recent lead-lag study, which was conducted in 2007, included several methodological 
flaws and needs to be updated.35  Vermont Gas disputed the Department’s characterization of the 
2007 lead-lag study, but it nonetheless did not object to conducting a new lead-lag study after 
consulting with the Department.36  Vermont Gas and the Department, therefore, agreed to the 
following proposed condition regarding a future lead-lag study: 
Vermont Gas shall perform a new lead lag study prior to filing its next traditional 
rate case and incorporate the results of that study in its determination of working 
capital. Prior to performing the new lead lag study, Vermont Gas shall confer with 
the Department regarding the study’s methodology.37

VII. 
ORDER 
IT IS HEREBY ORDERED, ADJUDGED, AND DECREED by the Public Utility Commission 
(“Commission”) of the State of Vermont that: 
1. Vermont Gas Systems, Inc. (“Vermont Gas”) may implement a rate increase of 
10.13% in daily access and distribution charges (“non-gas rate”) effective for bills rendered on or 
after November 1, 2023. 
2. Vermont Gas is required to use monies from the System Expansion and Reliability 
Fund (“SERF”) consistent with this Order. 
3. Within three business days of issuance of this Order, Vermont Gas shall file 
compliance tariffs reflecting changes as a result of this Order. 
4. Vermont Gas shall perform a new lead-lag study prior to filing its next traditional rate 
case and incorporate the results of that study in its determination of working capital.  Before 
performing the new lead-lag study, Vermont Gas shall confer with the Department regarding the 
study’s methodology.
